title: U.S. and China Agree to AI Hotline After Summit
summary:
President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump met for three days in Washington and agreed to set up a communication channel for AI-related incidents, plus a military crisis hotline. The summit didn't produce any huge breakthroughs, but analysts say the working groups could help stop small disputes from turning into big ones.

The two countries also agreed to keep talking about trade. China will import at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in 2027 and 2028. They will also keep working on rare earths — special metals used in electronics — after China put export controls on them last year.

Trump showed unusual warmth toward Xi, even though he had escalated a trade war the year before. But he made one thing clear: the U.S. won't slow its AI progress. "We're leading by at least a year, maybe a year and a half," Trump told reporters. "I'm not looking to open it up."

Both sides will meet again in November at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, and later at the G20 in Florida. They also agreed that Iran should not develop nuclear weapons and that no country should charge tolls on international waterways.

"Personal diplomacy between the two leaders is important, but the emphasis on working-level engagement... suggests an effort to make that stability more durable," said Wang Zichen of the Center for China and Globalization.
why_it_matters: Decisions made by these two governments shape the technology, jobs and products the next generation grows up with — and the new hotlines are meant to keep a rivalry from accidentally turning into a shooting war.

background_read: The United States and China are the world's two largest economies, and their relationship has swung between cooperation and open conflict for years. Donald Trump (the U.S. president, whose second term began in January 2025) put tariffs on Chinese goods during his first term, and China answered with tariffs of its own — a pattern that keeps pushing both sides back to the negotiating table.

Xi Jinping (China's president since 2013) has made technology and self-reliance a national priority, pouring money into AI and chip-making. Rare earths are part of that power: China refines most of the world's supply of these metals, so its export controls can slow factories in the U.S., Europe and Japan.

The two leaders will meet again at APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation — a yearly gathering of Pacific Rim economies, founded in 1989) in Shenzhen, a technology hub in southern China, and later at the G20 (a forum of the world's biggest economies).
Iran's nuclear programme has been a global flashpoint since the 2015 deal that limited it, which the U.S. later left — one reason both presidents now say Iran should not develop nuclear weapons.

perspectives.description: Diplomats and analysts see the AI channel, the military hotline and the new working groups as small but useful safety nets. The idea is that when ships or drones get too close, officials have a number to call instead of guessing. Wang Zichen argues this working-level engagement could make the stability between the two countries 'more durable'.

Sceptics point out the summit produced no huge breakthroughs: no big tariff deal and no end to the technology fight. The coal purchases are set for 2027 and 2028, so nothing changes right away, and Trump himself said the U.S. won't slow its AI progress. From this view, the warm photos matter more than the agreements.

U.S.-China trade fights have followed a pattern of escalation, partial truce and renewed friction for years. Summits often reset the tone without solving the underlying dispute over technology, metals and military power. At the same time, both leaders still need each other's cooperation on issues like Iran and shipping routes.

The real test comes at the APEC summit in Shenzhen and the G20 in Florida, where promises about coal and rare earths must turn into actual deals. Watch whether the military hotline is properly staffed and used, and whether the AI channel survives the next close call.
